newsitem.title: USA: Washington governor vetoes gay marriage ban.
newsitem.headline: Washington governor vetoes gay marriage ban.

text.p: Washington state Gov. Gary Locke Friday vetoed a bill banning same-sex marriages, calling it "divisive and unnecessary."

Leaders of the Republican-controlled state Legislature said they would attempt to override the Democratic governor's veto. If they failed, they vowed to place a referendum on gay marriage on the November statewide ballot.

"I will oppose measures that divide, disrespect or diminish our humanity," Locke wrote in his veto message. "Our overarching principle should be to promote civility, mutual respect and unity. This legislation fails to meet this test."

The vetoed measure defined marriage solely as a union between a man and a woman. As in many other states, legislative action was prompted out of concern that courts in Hawaii may legalise gay and lesbian marriages.
A district court in Honolulu is considering the appeal of a gay couple who claim the denial of the state to give them a marriage license violates their civil rights.

A final ruling from the Hawaiian Supreme Court is thought to be many months -- or possibly years -- away. The 1996 federal Defence of Marriage Act gave states the option to refuse to recognise same-sex marriages performed elsewhere.
Since the controversy in Hawaii erupted, 18 mainland states have passed legislation banning gay marriage.
A disappointed Republican House Speaker Clyde Ballard said Locke had failed to see the urgency created by the initial Hawaiian court rulings.

"What is the problem with passing the language," reaffirming old state court rulings prohibiting same-sex marriages, he asked. "By your non-action, you will be putting a stamp of approval on same-sex marriage."
Ballard doubted he could muster the votes to override the governor's veto in the House.

The Republicans' next step would be to place a referendum on the November ballot that asks voters to ban gay and lesbian unions. The only openly gay member of the Washington legislature, Democratic Representative Ed Murray of Seattle, decried that possibility.

"When you put these things on the ballot, you're asking for trouble," Murray said. "You're asking for a state to be torn apart, and I don't think the Republicans truly want to tear this state apart for the next year."
